note: General home-garden guidance written for LeafScan. Keys must match labels.json. Titles come from labels.json. Always check local extension advice and product labels.

pepper_bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas bacteria. It spreads in warm, wet weather through splashing water, handling wet plants, and infected seed or transplants. There is no cure for infected leaves; the goal is to slow the spread.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown and may look angular
Spots sometimes have a yellow halo and can merge into larger dead patches
Yellowing and early leaf drop, which can leave fruit exposed to sunscald
Raised, rough, scab-like spots on fruit
actions: Remove badly spotted leaves and bag them; do not compost them
Avoid working among plants while the foliage is wet
Water at the base of the plant instead of overhead
Clean pruners and stakes with a disinfectant after handling affected plants
Copper-based sprays may slow the spread if started early; follow the product label and local rules
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Choose resistant varieties where available
Rotate: avoid planting peppers or tomatoes in the same spot for 2-3 years
Remove plant debris at the end of the season

pepper_healthy.summary: No signs of the diseases this model knows about. Keep up good care and re-check regularly, including the undersides of leaves.
actions: Keep watering steady and at the base of the plant
Mulch to keep soil moisture even and reduce soil splash onto leaves
Check leaves weekly; early detection makes problems easier to manage
prevention: Give plants enough space for air to move between them
Rotate crop locations each year

potato_early_blight.summary: Early blight is a fungal disease (Alternaria) that usually starts on older, lower leaves and is worse on stressed plants in warm weather with heavy dew or rain. It weakens plants gradually rather than killing them quickly.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings, like a target, on older leaves
Spots often bordered by yellow tissue; affected leaves yellow and die
Damage moves upward through the plant over time
Tubers can develop dark, slightly sunken, dry lesions
actions: Remove heavily affected lower leaves and bag them
Water at the base, early in the day, so leaves dry quickly
Keep plants well fed and watered - stressed plants are more susceptible
Fungicides labelled for early blight can slow it; follow the label
prevention: Rotate: keep potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and eggplant out of the same bed for 2-3 years
Remove and destroy plant debris after harvest
Let tubers mature and handle them gently at harvest

potato_late_blight.summary: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) spreads very quickly in cool, humid or wet weather and can destroy foliage within days. It also infects tubers and spreads to nearby tomatoes and potatoes, so act promptly.
symptoms: Pale green to dark brown, water-soaked patches, often starting at leaf tips or edges
White, fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Dark lesions on stems; whole plants can collapse quickly
Tubers with reddish-brown, firm rot under the skin
actions: Remove and bag infected foliage or plants; do not compost them
Check nearby potatoes and tomatoes daily
If foliage is badly affected, remove it and wait before harvesting so tubers are less likely to be infected
Store only sound, undamaged tubers and check them during storage
Contact your local extension service - late blight outbreaks are often tracked regionally
prevention: Plant certified seed potatoes; never plant tubers saved from infected crops
Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles
Choose resistant varieties where available
Protective fungicides are used before infection in high-risk weather; follow the label

potato_healthy.summary: No signs of the diseases this model knows about. Keep monitoring, especially during cool, wet spells when late blight can appear.
actions: Earth up (hill) soil around stems so tubers stay covered
Water evenly at the base of plants
Check leaves weekly, including undersides
prevention: Use certified seed potatoes
Rotate crop locations each year

tomato_bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas bacteria and is favoured by warm, wet weather. It spreads by splashing water, handling wet plants and infected seed. Infected leaves cannot be cured; management focuses on slowing spread.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, often less than 3 mm across
Spots may have yellow halos and merge, causing leaves to yellow and drop
Small, raised, scabby spots on green fruit
actions: Remove badly affected leaves and bag them
Avoid overhead watering and don't handle plants when wet
Disinfect tools and stakes after use
Copper-based sprays may help slow spread if used early; follow the label
prevention: Start with disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate away from tomatoes and peppers for 2-3 years
Clear plant debris after the season

tomato_early_blight.summary: Early blight is a common fungal disease (Alternaria) that starts on the oldest leaves near the ground and moves upward. Warm, humid weather and soil splash help it spread.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric 'target' rings on lower, older leaves
Yellowing around the spots; affected leaves eventually die and drop
Dark lesions on stems, and leathery dark spots near the stem end of fruit
actions: Remove affected lower leaves and bag them
Mulch around plants to stop soil splashing onto leaves
Water at the base, ideally in the morning
Stake or cage plants and prune for air flow
Fungicides labelled for early blight can slow it; follow the label
prevention: Rotate tomatoes, potatoes, peppers and eggplant to a new bed for 2-3 years
Remove plant debris at season end
Choose tolerant varieties where available

sources.title: Early Blight - Tomato, Pest Management Guidelines

tomato_late_blight.summary: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) can kill tomato plants within days in cool, wet or humid weather and spreads to nearby tomatoes and potatoes. Act quickly.
symptoms: Large, irregular, pale green to dark brown, water-soaked patches on leaves
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides when humid
Dark brown lesions on stems
Firm, greasy-looking brown patches on fruit
actions: Remove and bag infected plants or parts; do not compost them
Check neighbouring tomatoes and potatoes daily
Avoid wetting foliage when watering
Contact your local extension service - outbreaks are often tracked regionally
prevention: Buy healthy transplants and inspect them before planting
Choose late-blight-resistant varieties where available
Protective fungicides are used before infection in high-risk weather; follow the label

sources.title: Late Blight - Tomato, Pest Management Guidelines

tomato_healthy.summary: No signs of the diseases this model knows about. Keep up good care and re-scan if new spots or yellowing appear.
actions: Water deeply and evenly at the base
Mulch to keep moisture even and reduce soil splash
Remove the lowest leaves that touch the soil
Check leaves weekly, including undersides
prevention: Stake or cage plants for air flow
Rotate crop locations each year
